correctness.rationale: If n=p^2, s(n)=p+1 cannot divide phi(n)=p(p-1). If n=pq with p<q primes, d=p+q+1=s(pq) and phi(pq)=(p-1)(d-p-2)=(p-1)d-(p-1)(p+2). Therefore phi(n)/s(n) is integral iff d|(p-1)(p+2); d>2p+1 enforces q>p and q=d-p-1 prime. This is a correct iff and covers every Omega(n)=2 case. Independently checked representative prime pairs and direct arithmetic for 133 and other database examples; no extrapolation from finite tests.

originality.rationale: FAILED: Banks and Luca (2007) already establish s(Pm)|(2 sigma(m)-m)phi(m) for counterbalanced Pm with P>prime factors of m (their equation 2.13). Specializing m=p and P=q gives p+q+1|(p+2)(p-1), the precise assigned divisor condition. The reverse implication is the immediate rewrite of phi(pq) modulo p+q+1; writing q=d-p-1 and d>2p+1 merely reparametrizes the criterion. The claim is thus the elementary special case and reverse algebraic restatement of an earlier theorem, not an independent original classification.
